lines.text: MENTAL HEALTH LIBRARY / CHAPTER 09
Relationships, Social
Connection, and Mental
Wellbeing
A practical, evidence-informed learning chapter for individuals, families,
students, and communities in Rwanda.
Document status
Version 1.0 | 11 November 2026 | English. This is public-facing educational draft content, not a
clinical assessment or personal treatment plan. Professional clinical, safeguarding, accessibility,
and Kinyarwanda/French reviews are pending.
Learning outcomes
• Describe how relationships and social connection can affect mental wellbeing.
• Distinguish loneliness, social isolation, solitude, and supportive connection.
• Recognize respect, reciprocity, healthy boundaries, and concerning interpersonal patterns.
• Practice communication, conflict resolution, and safe help-seeking skills.
• Identify when loneliness or relationship stress warrants professional support.
How to use this chapter
Read the sections in order, or choose a topic relevant to your situation. All scenarios are fictional.
Exercises are optional; skip any that feel unsafe, intrusive, or emotionally overwhelming. For
children, tailor activities with appropriate adult or professional guidance. This chapter does not
require disclosure of personal experiences.
01. Why relationships matter for mental health
People develop and maintain wellbeing through many forms of connection: friendships, family ties,
classmates, colleagues, neighbours, mentors, peers, and chosen communities. Supportive
relationships may offer comfort during setbacks, practical assistance, recognition, shared enjoyment,
and a sense of belonging. They are one among many influences on mental health, alongside biology,
life experiences, economic security, and access to healthcare [1-3].
Social connection is not measured only by the number of people in someone’s contacts. A person
may have many acquaintances but few relationships in which they feel safe and understood. Another
person may have a small circle and feel well supported. Relationship quality, reliability, and personal

choice matter.
Connection can protect wellbeing without guaranteeing that a person will never experience
depression, anxiety, or another mental health condition. Similarly, being socially isolated does not
prove someone has a disorder. [1-3]
02. Understanding social connection, loneliness,
isolation, and solitude
Social connection
Social connection describes the structure, functions, and quality of how people relate to others.
Structure includes who is in a person’s network and how often they interact. Function includes the
type of emotional or practical support exchanged. Quality concerns whether interactions feel
supportive, trustworthy, strained, or harmful. This three-part explanation follows the WHO
social-connection framework [1].
Loneliness
Loneliness is a distressing feeling that occurs when a person experiences a gap between the
relationships they want and those they believe they have. A person can feel lonely in a crowded
classroom, busy workplace, or household. Loneliness is not a character flaw or proof of unpopularity
Social isolation
Social isolation refers to having relatively few relationships, social roles, or interactions. It may result
from geographic distance, disability-related barriers, bereavement, discrimination, relocation, low
income, or other circumstances. Someone can be isolated without feeling lonely, although the two
often overlap [1].
Solitude
Solitude is time spent alone, sometimes intentionally and comfortably. Quiet time for rest, prayer,
creative work, or reflection can be valuable. Being alone is not automatically unhealthy. What
matters is whether the person can access the level and quality of connection they need.
Reflection
Which word best describes your current experience: connected, lonely, isolated, enjoying solitude,
or unsure? There is no right answer. You may experience more than one at the same time.
03. Healthy relationships: what to look for
A healthy relationship is not a relationship without disagreements. It is one in which people can
disagree, grow, and make choices while preserving one another’s dignity. Healthy relationships may
include:

• Respect: each person’s needs, privacy, identity, and decisions are taken seriously.
• Trust: promises are generally kept; questions can be discussed without intimidation.
• Mutuality: both parties have room to speak, give, receive, and make choices; equal contribution is
not required every day.
• Boundaries: people can say no, request time apart, and change their mind.
• Support: care is offered without making the other person responsible for every emotion or problem.
• Repair: after mistakes, people can acknowledge harm, take responsibility, and change behaviour.
Family, friendship, romantic, and professional relationships have different expectations. The same
principle applies across them: caring for someone does not authorize monitoring, humiliating,
isolating, or coercing them.
04. Social support: emotional, practical, informational,
and belonging
People need different kinds of support at different times. Emotional support involves empathy and
being listened to. Practical support may include help with transportation, childcare, or sharing a task.
Informational support involves reliable guidance or help finding services. Belonging comes from
being part of a group in which a person feels accepted [2,3].
A student worried about examinations may benefit from a peer who listens, a tutor who helps
organise revision, and a trusted adult who notices exhaustion. No single person has to meet all those
needs. Developing more than one safe connection can reduce dependence on an individual
relationship.
Offering support should not become pressure. Ask what someone wants before giving advice,
involving others, or sharing a private situation.
05. Why making and maintaining connections can be
difficult
Challenges such as moving to a new district, unemployment, heavy school workloads,
disability-related access barriers, caregiving, bereavement, social anxiety, experiences of
discrimination, or limited money for transport can make maintaining relationships difficult. This is not
evidence that a person is unwilling or incapable of friendship.
Some people also need more time alone than others. The goal is not to force sociability or make
everyone attend large gatherings. It is to support meaningful relationships that fit individual
preferences and safety.
When a person has been hurt or controlled in a relationship, rebuilding trust may require time and
professional support. Encouraging immediate reconnection with unsafe individuals can increase risk.

06. Listening and communicating with care
Communication is not just about speaking clearly. It also involves checking what someone means,
allowing silence, and noticing whether the conversation feels safe. Helpful skills can be practised
gradually.
A four-step conversation method
• Choose a suitable moment. Ask whether the other person has time and privacy to talk.
• Describe what you observed without making an accusation: “I noticed we have barely spoken this
week.”
• Explain your feeling or need using “I” language: “I miss our conversations and would like to
reconnect.”
• Invite a response: “How has the week been for you?” Listen before deciding what to do next.
An “I” statement can make concerns easier to discuss, but it is not a guaranteed way to resolve
conflict. If the other person threatens or intimidates you, communication techniques are not a
substitute for safety planning.
Active listening
Active listening involves giving attention, avoiding unnecessary interruption, reflecting the meaning
of what someone says, and asking permission before offering advice. A supportive reply may sound
like: “That sounds exhausting. Would you prefer that I listen or help you think about options?”
07. Interpersonal conflict and healthy repair
Disagreements can arise from expectations, stress, financial strain, misunderstandings, or different
priorities. Constructive conflict management includes slowing down, focusing on a specific issue,
allowing each person a voice, agreeing on a realistic next step, and revisiting the matter when calm.
For instance, two housemates may disagree over shared chores. They could identify the tasks,
discuss what each can realistically manage, write down a fair arrangement, and review it after a
week. The goal is not winning an argument but developing a workable agreement.
Safety distinction
Ordinary disagreement is not the same as intimidation, coercive control, stalking, threats, or
violence. If a person feels unsafe, avoid encouraging joint confrontation, mediation, or couples
exercises as a default. Seek appropriate specialist assistance instead.

08. Emotional boundaries and personal autonomy
Boundaries are limits that protect time, privacy, emotional energy, and personal choices. A boundary
is not a punishment; it describes what a person can accept and what they will do to care for
themselves. Examples include choosing when to answer messages, deciding what information to
share, asking before discussing a sensitive topic, and refusing to lend money one cannot afford to
lose.
A respectful boundary might be: “I cannot talk about this during work. I can speak after 6 p.m.”
Another might be: “I am not ready to discuss that experience.” Setting a boundary does not
guarantee another person will respect it. In unsafe relationships, personal safety should take priority
over explaining a boundary repeatedly.
Emotional support does not mean becoming someone’s clinician, remaining available every hour, or
keeping dangerous secrets. It is appropriate to seek extra help when a problem exceeds what a
friend or family member can safely manage.
09. Loneliness and its effects on wellbeing
Prolonged loneliness and isolation are associated with poorer mental and physical health, although
the relationship is complex and not all individuals are affected in the same way [1-4]. Loneliness may
involve sadness, restlessness, reduced motivation, difficulty trusting others, or the sense that one is
disconnected even while surrounded by people.
Noticing loneliness can be a useful signal that a need for connection is unmet. It should not be
treated as a diagnosis. A person whose loneliness occurs alongside persistent low mood, anxiety,
sleep disturbance, or substantial impairment may benefit from professional assessment.
Gentle steps toward connection
• Identify one person or community setting that has previously felt reasonably safe.
• Choose a small action, such as a brief greeting, a message, or attending one group activity.
• Prefer shared interests over pressure to disclose private feelings.
• Repeat contact at a manageable pace; friendships often develop through time.
• If a group does not feel welcoming or safe, it is acceptable to try another setting.
10. Digital relationships and online wellbeing
Messaging apps, online learning groups, and social platforms can help people stay connected across
long distances. They can also create pressure to respond immediately, comparisons with others,
misunderstandings, or exposure to harassment. The quality and safety of an interaction matter more
than whether it happens online or in person.
Useful digital boundaries include asking before sharing someone else’s photo or story, respecting
delayed replies, choosing privacy settings thoughtfully, and avoiding arguments in public comment
sections when a private conversation would be safer. Digital access may not be private for someone
whose device is monitored.

If someone is being threatened or monitored, changing settings or blocking a contact might alert the
person causing harm. Specialist digital safety support may be needed before taking action.
11. Families, friends, peers, and caregivers
Families and caregivers can support wellbeing through reliable attention, predictable care,
encouragement, and help during difficulties. Friends and peers may provide acceptance and shared
experiences. Teachers, mentors, health workers, and community members may also become
valuable sources of support.
However, not every family or community relationship is safe. People should not be encouraged to
disclose private mental health concerns to relatives, religious leaders, or peers without considering
trust, confidentiality, and personal choice.
For adolescents, safe relationships with trusted adults are important. Adults should listen
respectfully, avoid dismissing concerns as “just a phase,” and seek appropriate professional or
safeguarding assistance when serious risks arise [3,5].
12. Community belonging in Rwanda
In Rwanda, possible opportunities for social connection may include school clubs, youth groups,
sports teams, community activities, volunteer initiatives, faith communities, study circles,
neighbourhood associations, and peer-support programmes. These are illustrative settings, not
guaranteed services or endorsements.
Participation should remain voluntary. Activities should be inclusive of people with disabilities,
individuals living far from community centres, people with limited connectivity, and those who may
not feel safe in some groups. Privacy and protection from stigma are especially important when
mental health is discussed.
Community programmes can support connection by providing accessible meeting places, predictable
schedules, welcoming facilitators, and a way to raise concerns safely [1,2].
13. Supporting someone who feels lonely or distressed
Begin by asking how the person would like to be supported. Offer specific, practical options instead
of making broad promises. For example: “Would you like me to check in this weekend?” or “Would it
help to walk together after class?” Respect a no and avoid turning an invitation into pressure.
Do not assume that frequent contact is always best. Some people need time, rest, or privacy. If a
person speaks about hopelessness, self-harm, or suicide, take it seriously and seek appropriate
urgent professional support. Do not promise to keep an immediate safety risk secret.

14. When professional support is appropriate
Consider consultation with a qualified healthcare or mental health professional when loneliness,
social withdrawal, or interpersonal stress becomes persistent, overwhelming, or interferes with
sleep, school, employment, or daily responsibilities; when anxiety or depression symptoms are
present; or when repeated conflict or trauma makes it difficult to feel safe.
Urgent assistance is needed when there is immediate danger, threats of serious violence, or concern
that someone may act on thoughts of suicide or self-harm. Seek available emergency medical
assistance or the nearest appropriate emergency facility. Specific Rwanda contacts and operating
hours must be confirmed before publication of this chapter.
15. Fictional learning scenarios
Scenario A — A first-year university student in Kigali
A student moved from Musanze for university. Although they speak with many classmates, they feel
they have no one to rely on. They decide to attend a small study group twice and message a former
school friend. Discussion: Why can someone be lonely around other people? What makes a
manageable first step?
Scenario B — A parent balancing work and caregiving
A parent with long working hours has little opportunity to meet friends. Instead of committing to
several activities, they arrange a short weekly call with a trusted person and ask whether a
neighbour can occasionally help with a practical task. Discussion: What barriers make connection
difficult? How can support include practical help?
Scenario C — Two friends disagree
One friend feels ignored when replies arrive late. The other explains they often share a phone and
have limited data. They agree not to interpret slow replies as rejection and decide on a regular time
to catch up. Discussion: How did assumptions influence the disagreement?
Scenario D — Pressure within a relationship
A person’s partner demands their phone password, discourages friendships, and becomes angry
when they attend a community event. A trusted mentor suggests individual specialist support rather
than an immediate confrontation. Discussion: Which behaviours go beyond ordinary disagreement,
and why does safety come first?
Scenario E — A community sports group
A newcomer wants to join a local sports team but worries about not fitting in. The organizer explains
expectations kindly, allows the person to observe initially, and provides an accessible way to ask
questions. Discussion: How does a welcoming environment strengthen belonging?

16. Guided educational activities
Activity 1 — My support map (10–15 minutes)
On paper, draw three circles labelled “People I trust,” “Places or groups I may choose,” and
“Professional services if needed.” Add only contacts you genuinely consider safe. Do not include
identifying information if someone else may see the page. A blank circle is not a failure; it identifies a
possible area to build gradually.
Activity 2 — Connection without pressure (7 days)
Choose a low-risk, realistic action: send a greeting, attend one community activity, sit with a
classmate at lunch, or reconnect with a trustworthy acquaintance. Afterward, note how comfortable
it felt, whether the interaction was respectful, and whether you want to repeat it. Stop or adapt the
exercise if it increases distress or risk.
Activity 3 — Listening practice
With a willing and trusted partner, take turns speaking about a neutral topic for two minutes. The
listener does not interrupt and asks one clarifying question. Then switch roles. Reflect on the
difference between listening and immediately solving a problem. Do not use sensitive trauma
disclosures for this exercise.
Activity 4 — Boundary sentence
Write a simple statement that describes a limit without blaming another person: “I need some time
before discussing this” or “I prefer not to share my account password.” You do not need to deliver it
to someone if that would be unsafe.
Activity 5 — Community inclusion audit
Think of a school club, sports group, or community event. Ask: Can people attend with limited money
or transport? Are newcomers welcomed? Can someone leave without pressure? Are disability needs
considered? Is private information protected? Identify one change that could make the activity safer
and more inclusive.
17. Knowledge assessment
1. Can a person feel lonely despite having many social contacts? Yes. Loneliness is about perceived
unmet connection needs, not only the number of contacts.
2. Are solitude and loneliness identical? No. Solitude may be chosen and restorative, while loneliness
involves distress.
3. Name two elements of a healthy relationship. Examples: respect, trust, boundaries, mutuality,
support, or repair after mistakes.
4. What is one example of practical social support? Help with transportation, childcare, or completing
a necessary task.

5. What does active listening involve? Attention, respectful questions, reflection, and not interrupting
unnecessarily.
6. Does an argument always mean abuse? No. However, threats, coercion, intimidation, or
controlling patterns warrant safety attention.
7. Is sharing a friend’s personal story online acceptable without asking? No. Seek informed
permission and respect privacy.
8. Must someone attend large social gatherings to be mentally healthy? No. Connection needs and
preferences vary.
9. What should you do if setting a boundary could trigger danger? Prioritise safety and seek
appropriate professional or specialist guidance.
10. When might loneliness warrant professional support? When persistent or accompanied by
significant distress, impaired functioning, or other concerning symptoms.
18. Summary and key messages
• Supportive relationships contribute to wellbeing, but people need different types and amounts of
connection.
• Loneliness is a feeling; social isolation refers to limited interactions; solitude can be chosen.
• Quality, respect, boundaries, and safety matter as much as contact frequency.
• Small, repeatable, voluntary social actions may be more useful than pressured participation.
• A safe relationship allows disagreement without intimidation or coercion.
• Professional care is appropriate when distress persists or functioning is affected.
19. Glossary
Social connection: Relationships and interactions considered in terms of structure, support function, and quality.
Loneliness: Distress caused by a perceived gap between desired and existing connections.
Social isolation: Relatively few social relationships or interactions.
Emotional boundary: A limit around emotional availability, disclosure, or personal responsibility.
Active listening: Attentive, respectful listening aimed at understanding rather than immediately judging or fixing.
Coercive control: A pattern of intimidation or restrictions used to dominate another person.
Belonging: Feeling accepted and valued as part of a relationship or group.

Evidence note: The chapter paraphrases official source guidance and adds original, fictional scenarios and

as a clinical intervention. No local referral contact is asserted as verified in this version.
Publication review checklist
Before public release: (1) clinical review; (2) safeguarding and domestic-violence safety review;
(3) fact-check of references and Rwanda-specific services; (4) plain-language and accessibility
review; (5) culturally appropriate Kinyarwanda/French translations; (6) version control and
scheduled review date.
